articles.title: नेपालमा एक वर्षमै ६१ हजारभन्दा बढी मुद्दा, औसतमा दैनिक १६७ अपराध दर्ता
articles.summary:
नेपालमा एक वर्षको अवधिमा ६१ हजारभन्दा बढी आपराधिक मुद्दा दर्ता भएका छन् ।

नेपाल प्रहरीले आर्थिक वर्ष २०८२/८३ को वार्षिक कार्यप्रगति विवरण सार्वजनिक गर्दै एक वर्षमा कुल ६१ हजार १६ वटा मुद्दा दर्ता भएको जनाएको हो । प्रहरीका अनुसार यो संख्या अघिल्लो आर्थिक वर्षको तुलनामा बढेको हो। आर्थिक वर्ष २०८१/८२ मा ५८ हजार ४७२ मुद्दा दर्ता भएकोमा २०८२/८३ मा यो संख्या बढेर ६१ हजार १६ पुगेको छ।

प्रहरीको तथ्यांकअनुसार औसतमा दैनिक १६७ वटा मुद्दा दर्ता हुने गरेको छ। सबैभन्दा धेरै मुद्दा बैंकिङ कसुरतर्फ देखिएको छ। एक वर्षमा बैंकिङ कसुरका १२ हजार ९५० मुद्दा दर्ता भएका छन्। त्यसपछि सार्वजनिक हित, स्वास्थ्य, सुरक्षा, सुविधा र नैतिकताविरुद्धका ८ हजार ७०७ कसुर दर्ता भएका छन्।

आत्महत्यासम्बन्धी घटना ६ हजार १९७, लागूऔषधसम्बन्धी ५ हजार ७९१ र साधारण चोरीका ३ हजार ५२४ मुद्दा दर्ता भएका छन्। जबरजस्ती करणीका २ हजार ३८०, ठगी, आपराधिक विश्वासघात तथा आपराधिक लाभसम्बन्धी २ हजार ३७५ र सवारी ज्यानसम्बन्धी २ हजार ९४ मुद्दा दर्ता भएका छन्।

प्रहरीको विवरणले नेपालमा अपराधको प्रकृति परम्परागत चोरी, हिंसा र अन्य अपराधसँगै आर्थिक तथा लागूऔषधजन्य कसुरतर्फ पनि गम्भीर चुनौती देखाइरहेको संकेत गरेको छ। प्रदेशगत रूपमा काठमाडौं उपत्यकामा सबैभन्दा धेरै १५ हजार २९७ मुद्दा दर्ता भएका छन्। मधेशमा १० हजार ७५० र कोशीमा ९ हजार ८६३ मुद्दा दर्ता भएका छन्।

articles.title: माङसेबुङका ११ विद्यालयमा लिम्बू र वान्तवा भाषा अनिवार्य
articles.summary:
इलाम जिल्लाको माङसेबुङ गाउँपालिकाले ११ वटा सामुदायिक विद्यालयमा लिम्बू र वान्तवा भाषा अनिवार्य गरेको छ।

गाउँपालिकाले राई समुदायका विद्यार्थीको बाहुल्य रहेका तीनवटा विद्यालयमा यसै शैक्षिक सत्रदेखि वान्तवा भाषा तथा लिम्बू समुदायका विद्यार्थीको बाहुल्य रहेका थप तीनवटा विद्यालयमा लिम्बू भाषा पाठ्यपुस्तक अनिवार्य विषयका रूपमा लागु गरेको हो। यसअघि चारवटा विद्यालयमा लिम्बू र एउटा विद्यालयमा वान्तवा भाषा अध्यापन हुँदै आएको थियो।

शिक्षा शाखा प्रमुख बुद्धिप्रसाद खतिवडाका अनुसार माङसेबुङ–२ स्थित सरस्वती आधारभूत विद्यालय, माङसेबुङ–४ स्थित जनता आधारभूत विद्यालय र माङसेबुङ–६ स्थित सिंहेश्वरी आधारभूत विद्यालयमा यस वर्षदेखि वान्तवा भाषा पाठ्यपुस्तक लागु गरिएको हो। यसअघि माङसेबुङ–६ स्थित चिसोपानी माध्यमिक विद्यालयमा मात्र वान्तवा भाषा पठनपाठन हुँदै आएको थियो। यसैगरी, माङसेबुङ–१ स्थित गजुरमुखी आधारभूत विद्यालय र मण्डिका आधारभूत विद्यालय तथा माङसेबुङ–३ स्थित दुर्गा माध्यमिक विद्यालयमा यस वर्षदेखि लिम्बू भाषा पाठ्यपुस्तक लागु गरिएको छ।

यसअघि माङसेबुङ–३ स्थित पवित्रा आधारभूत विद्यालय तथा माङसेबुङ–५ स्थित साम्जिक मुन्धुम आधारभूत विद्यालय, सरस्वती माध्यमिक विद्यालय र साम्जिक मुन्धुम पाठशालामा लिम्बू भाषा पढाइ हुँदै आएको थियो। मातृभाषा लागु भएका विद्यालयमा गाउँपालिकाले आन्तरिक स्रोतबाट तलबभत्ता उपलब्ध गराउने गरी शिक्षक दरबन्दी सिर्जना गरेर शिक्षकको व्यवस्था गरेको छ।

गाउँपालिका अध्यक्ष हेमन्त राईले प्रत्येक समुदायलाई आफ्नो मातृभाषामा विद्यालय तथा शैक्षिक संस्था सञ्चालनको अधिकार संविधानले दिएको सम्झाउँदै सोहीअनुसार मातृभाषा शिक्षालाई प्राथमिकता दिइएको बताए। 'हामीले नयाँ शैक्षिक संस्था त खोलेनौँ, सामुदायिक बाहुल्य भएको विद्यालयमा मातृभाषा शिक्षकको दरबन्दी सिर्जना गरी मातृभाषा पाठ्यपुस्तक लागु गरेर पठनपाठन गराएका हौँ,' अध्यक्ष राईले भने।

मातृभाषा शिक्षा लागु नभएका अन्य विद्यालयमा स्थानीय पाठ्यपुस्तक ‘हाम्रो माङसेबुङ’ अध्यापन हुँदै आएको छ। माङसेबुङ गाउँपालिकाले गत जेठ १२ गतेदेखि गाउँपालिकाभर लिम्बू भाषालाई सरकारी कामकाजको भाषा घोषणा गरी लागु गरेको छ।

articles.title: सत्ताको प्राथमिकतामा किन पर्दैन सञ्चार क्षेत्र?
articles.summary:
चैत १३ गते मुलुकको कार्यकारी प्रमुख प्रधानमन्त्रीको जिम्मेवारी समालेका बालेन्द्र शाहले पहिलो पटक साउन १० गते राष्ट्रका नाममा सम्बोधन गरे। मुलुकको समसामयिक विषयमा होइन, सुनसरीको देवानगन्ज–३ स्थित कप्तानगन्जमा भएको दुई पक्षीय विवादको आगो तराई मधेसमा पनि सल्कन थालेपछि प्रधानमन्त्रीले सम्बोधन गरेका हुन्। त्यो पनि प्रधानमन्त्री शाहले आमसञ्चारका माध्यमहरूलाई बोलाएर वा पत्रकार सम्मेलन गरेर होइन, आफ्नै सामाजिक सञ्जालमार्फत पहिलो सम्बोधन सार्वजनिक गरे।

सरकार नियन्त्रित सार्वजनिक सेवा प्रसारण नेपाल (नेपाल टेलिभिजन) ले प्रधानमन्त्री शाहको सम्बोधन रेकर्ड गरेको थियो। तर प्रधानमन्त्रीलाई निजी सञ्चार क्षेत्रमाथि त विश्वास लागेन नै, राज्य नियन्त्रित संस्थामाथि पनि भरोसा भएन। त्यसैले त उनले नेपाल टेलिभिजनबाट आफ्नो सम्बोधन प्रसारणपूर्व झन्डै दुई मिनेट (१.५७ सेकेन्ड) अघि नै सामाजिक सञ्जाल फेसबुकमा राखे। स्थानीय तहको निर्वाचनअघि सञ्चारगृहमा गएर अन्तर्वार्ता दिएका शाहले काठमाडौं महानगरपालिकाको मेयरको जिम्मेवारीमा पुगेपछि नेपाली सञ्चारमाध्यममा कार्यरत पत्रकारलाई अन्तर्वार्ता होइन, भेट्न पनि आवश्यक ठानेनन्। अहिले मुलुकको प्रधानमन्त्रीको जिम्मेवारीमा रहेका शाहले सरकारमातहतका निकायलाई पनि विश्वास नगरेको स्पष्ट हुन्छ। जबकि प्रधानमन्त्री शाहको पार्टी राष्ट्रिय स्वतन्त्र पार्टी (रास्वपा) का सभापति रवि लामिछानको करिअर नै सञ्चारकर्मीका रूपमा निर्माण हुँदै अहिलेको अवस्थामा पुगेका हुन्।

लामिछाने मात्र होइन, शाह नेतृत्वको सरकारमा सहभागी कम्तीमा तीन मन्त्रीको पृष्ठभूमि पनि सञ्चारकर्मीकै छ। उनीहरू मात्र होइन, रास्वपाबाट अहिले प्रतिनिधिसभा प्रतिनिधित्व गर्ने दुई दर्जन बढी सदस्यले पनि यही क्षेत्रबाट आफ्नो करिअर सुरु गरेका हुन्। अहिले उनीहरू नै संसद्मा दुई तिहाइ बहुमतनजिक छन् भने सरकारमा पनि रास्वपा नै छ। यस क्षेत्रलाई बुझेका मात्र होइन, भोगेकाहरूबाट नेपाली सञ्चार क्षेत्र र सञ्चारकर्मीहरूले सुधार तथा सकारात्मक विभेदको अपेक्षा राखेका थिए र छन्।

फागुन २१ गतेको निर्वाचनपछिको यो अवधिमा रास्वपा र उसको नेतृत्व सरकारको प्राथमिकतामा आमसञ्चार क्षेत्र परेको छैन। सामाजिक सञ्जालहरूलाई नै जनतासम्म पुग्ने साध्य र साधनका रूपमा उपयोग गर्दै आएका उनीहरूको सञ्चारकर्मी र सञ्चार क्षेत्रलाई हेर्ने दृष्टिकोण भने पुराना राजनीतिक दल र अरू क्षेत्रबाट आएका नेताहरूको भन्दा पनि अनुदार देखिएको छ।

हुन त २०७९ मंसिरमा भएको निर्वाचनबाट रास्वपा चौथो शक्तिका रूपमा उदाएको थियो। त्यससँगै रास्वपा सभापति लामिछाने उपप्रधान तथा गृहमन्त्रीको जिम्मेवरीमा पुगे। निर्वाचनअघिदेखि नै उनको नागरिकतासहितका विषयमा सञ्चारमाध्यमले निरन्तर प्रश्न उठाएका थिए र पछि सर्वोच्च अदालतले उनको सबै पद नै खारेज गरिदियो। फेरि नागरिकता लिएर उपनिर्वाचनमा प्रतिस्पर्धा गरेका लामिछानेले पार्टी कार्यालयमा पत्रकार सम्मेलन गरेर सञ्चारमाध्यम र सञ्चारकर्मीका विषयमा ‘विष नै वमन’ गरेका थिए। मूलधारका सम्पादकहरूको नामै उल्लेख गरेर उनले ‘१२ भाइ’ भन्ने भाष्य निर्माण गरे। आफ्ना कमजोरी उजागर हुँदा विगतमा पनि लामिछानेले जस्तै अन्य राजनीतिक दल र तिनका नेताहरूले मात्र होइन, अन्य पेसा र व्यवसायका मान्छेहरू पनि पत्रकार र पत्रकारिता प्रतिप्रश्न उठाएर पन्छिने गरेका थिए र छन्।

यसको मतलब पत्रकारिता क्षेत्रमा समस्या नै छैन भन्ने होइन, समस्या छन्। अहिले हातमा बुम बोकेपछि जसलाई जे पनि भन्न र गर्न पाइन्छ भन्ने मान्यता विकास भएको छ। भ्युजकारिताले अधिकारको मात्र कुरा गर्ने जिम्मेवारीबोध र कर्तव्यबोध हराउँदै जाँदा पत्रकारिताको साख मात्र गिराएको छैन, गुमाइएको पनि छ।

नेपाल पत्रकार महासंघका पूर्वअध्यक्ष शिव गाउँले केही साताअघि महासंघको राष्ट्रिय भेलामा यही कुरा सुनाउँदै भनेका थिए, ‘प्रेस पास र पत्रकारिताका औजारहरू पछिल्ला दिनमा शक्ति प्रदर्शन गर्ने साधन’ बनाइएका छन्। ती त समाजलाई सुसूचित गर्ने र जनताका कथा ल्याएर सत्ता वा शक्तिलाई जवाफदेही बनाउने साधन मात्रै हुन् भन्दै उनले भनेका थिए, ‘यो शक्ति प्रदर्शन गर्ने अहंकार पत्रकारिताको आचरण र नैतिकताभित्र पर्दैन।’

अहिले बुम र क्यामेराको अहंकार चर्को गरी सामना गर्नुपरेको पनि उनको बुझाइ थियो। पत्रकारिताले मूलतः जनताका प्रश्नहरूको प्रतिनिधित्व गरेर सत्ता वा शक्तिबाट त्यसको जवाफ माग्नुपर्ने हो। तर अहिले पत्रकारिताका धेरै प्रश्नले जनताको चाहना वा रुचि बोक्न छाडेका छन्।

तत्कालीन मुद्दा थाहा नपाउने, अगाडि जो भेट्यो उसैलाई जे पायो त्यही सोध्ने र अझ कार्यक्रममा बोलाइएका अतिथिलाई सक्दो मानमर्दन गरेर अपमानित गरेर उसको उछित्तो काढेर पछि मात्र सेलिब्रेटी पत्रकार भइन्छ भन्ने मनोविज्ञान विकास भएको छ। यसको गम्भीर असर पत्रकारले गर्ने प्रश्नमा जनताको भावना नभेटिँदा हाम्रा प्रश्नहरू कमजोर र कतिपय अवस्थामा निकम्मा हुँदै गएको गाउँलेको बुझाइ छ। यसले हाम्रा प्रश्नहरूको कुनै मूल्य र महत्त्व छैन भन्ने सन्देश जनतामा गएको जनाउँदै उनले थपे, ‘पत्रकारका प्रश्नहरू कमजोर भएपछि पत्रकारिता कहाँ बलियो हुन्छ?’

पत्रकारले नै आफ्ना प्रश्नहरू कमजोर बनाइरहेका छन् भने प्रविधिले ल्याएको अवसर अर्थात् डिजिटल प्ल्याटफर्महरू त्यसका लागि सहयोगी बनेका छन्। पत्रकार र पत्रकारिताका विषयमा उठेका प्रश्नको जवाफ अरू पेसा, व्यवसाय र क्षेत्रका मान्छेले होइन, यही क्षेत्रले दिनुपर्छ। आफ्नो पेसा र व्यवसायप्रति विश्वास जागृत गर्न यही पेस र व्यवसायमा रहेकाले गल्ती सच्याउने र सच्चिने तत्परता देखाउनुपर्छ। आमसञ्चार माध्यम र पत्रकार को हो को होइन भन्ने बहस चलिरहेका बेला यसको पुनः परिभाषित गर्नुपर्ने पनि कतिपयको बुझाइ र विश्लेषण छ।

एउटा पत्रकार, सम्पादक वा सञ्चारगृह नागरिकका प्रश्नबाट विमुख हुन पाउँदैन। ऊ सधैं जवाफदेही र जिम्मेवार बन्नुपर्छ। आजका दिनमा अपवादबाहेकका सञ्चारकर्मी र सञ्चारगृह त्यसबाट विमुख रहेको आरोप लाग्ने गरेको छ। एउट सञ्चारगृह हुन के के योग्यता, क्षेमता र जनशक्ति चाहिन्छ ? त्यसले उत्पादन गर्ने सञ्चार सामग्रीहरू प्रशोधन त्यसअनुसार भएका छन् कि छैनन्, अहिलेको सबैभन्दा ठुलो प्रश्न त्यही र त्यहीँ छ।

पत्रकार र सञ्चारगृहका मात्र होइन, यस क्षेत्रमा काम गर्ने संघसंस्था र सरकारको पनि यस क्षेत्रको विकास र विस्तारमा ध्यान पुगेको छैन। विपक्षमा हुँदा सञ्चारमाध्यमलाई उपयोग गर्न उद्यत् हुने राजनीतिक दलहरू सत्तामा गएपछि नियन्त्रण गर्न सक्रिय हुने पुरानै परिपाटी हो।

अहिलेको सरकारले नियन्त्रण होइन, बेवास्ता गर्दै सामाजिक सञ्जाललाई नै सञ्चारको टुल्सका रूपमा उपयोग गर्दै आएको छ तर यस क्षेत्रको विकास, विस्तार र व्यवस्थित गर्न सरकारको कुनै चासो र चिन्ता देखिएको छैन। वर्षौं पुराना कानुनहरूको अध्यावधिक मात्र होइन, सामाजिक सञ्जाललाई नियमन गर्ने कानुन निर्माण गर्नुपर्ने आवश्यकता छ। पुरातन ढंग र ढर्राबाट पत्रपत्रिकाको वर्गीकरण हुँदै आएका छन्। त्यसको सुधार मात्र होइन, असरल्ल सञ्चलनामा रहेका सञ्चारमाध्यमको वर्गीकरण गर्नुपर्ने आवश्यकता विज्ञहरूले औल्याउँदै आएका छन्।

कुनै समय हावा भरिएको बेलुनजस्ता सञ्चार गृहहरू विज्ञापन बजारमा आएको संकुचनसँगै अहिले हावा फुस्केका बेलुनजस्तो बन्न पुगेका छन्। यसले सञ्चारमाध्यममा श्रम समस्या विकराल बन्दै गएको र सञ्चार संस्था टिकाइराख्न पनि धौधौ परेको देखाउँछ।

हिजो राजनीतिक दलहरू संकटमा पर्दा र लोकतान्त्रिक प्रक्रिया अवरुद्ध हुँदा नेपालका पत्रकार र सञ्चार उद्योगले महत्त्वपूर्ण योगदान गरेको थियो र अहिले पनि गर्दै आएको छ तर अहिले सञ्चार क्षेत्र संकटग्रस्त बन्दै जाँदा यस क्षेत्रका विषयमा सरकार र सरोकारवाला निकायहरूको चिन्ता र चिन्तन देखिएको छैन।

सञ्चारकर्मीको मात्र होइन, सञ्चारमाध्यमको पनि विकास र विस्तारलगायतको विषय उठानको अगुवाइ नेपाल पत्रकार महासंघले गर्नुपर्ने हो। पत्रकारहरू क्षमता अभिवृद्धि, सेवासुविधा र अधिकार मात्र होइन, कर्तव्यबोध गराउने भूमिका महासंघसहितका संघसंस्थाले निर्वाह गर्नुपर्ने हो।

त्यति मात्र होइन, पत्रकार, प्रकाशक/सञ्चालक र सरकारसँग यस क्षेत्रका समस्या, विकास र विस्तारमा उसको अहं भूमिका हुनुपर्छ र हुन्छ तर श्रमको मुद्दालाई मात्र उसले बोक्दा पत्रकार र सञ्चालक/प्रकाशकबिचमा पुलको भूमिका निर्वाह गर्नुपर्ने पत्रकार महासंघ र सञ्चालक/प्रकाशक भैंसीदेखि जोगी र जोगीदेखि भैंसी डराउनेजस्तो बन्न पुगेका छन्। जसले सञ्चार गृह र पत्रकारहरू खासखास समस्या के–के हुन् र कसरी समाधान गर्न सकिन्छ भन्ने बहस र छलफल हुनै सकेको छैन। श्रमदेखि यस क्षेत्रका समस्याको दीर्घकालीन समाधानका लागि नीति निर्माणमा लाग्नुपर्ने महासंघ धर्ना र जुलुसमा सीमित हुन पुगेको छ। त्यसले तत्काल कुनै घटना विशेषलाई सम्बोधन गरेर पनि रोगको उपचार नहुँदा महासंघप्रति पत्रकारहरूकै विश्वास कमजोर बन्दै गएको छ।

त्यससँगै सञ्चारमाध्यम वा गृहहरू उद्योग हो कि सोसल सर्भिस भन्ने प्रश्न र बहस पनि सुरु भएको छ। उद्योग हो भने अन्य उद्योगमा जस्तै यस क्षेत्रमा पनि पुँजी, बजार, श्रमिकको सुनिश्चितता नभई दर्ता भएर मात्र वा त्यतिकै सञ्चालन गर्न पाइने कि नपाइने ? त्यसका लागि निश्चित लगानीको सुनिश्चितता चाहिन्छ कि चाहिँदैन भन्ने प्रश्न उठ्न थालेको छ। होइन यो सोसल सर्भिस हो भने यसबाट व्यापार–व्यवसाय मात्र होइन, यसले आर्जन गरेको सम्पत्ति व्यक्तिको हुने कि नहुने? त्यति मात्र होइन, श्रम ऐन कि श्रमजीवी पत्रकार ऐन कार्यान्वयन गर्ने भन्ने विवाद र बहस पनि सँगै आएको छ।

articles.title: पाकिस्तान, टर्की र साउदी अरेबियाबिच रक्षा सम्झौता
articles.summary:
पाकिस्तान, टर्की र साउदी अरेबियाले पारस्परिक रक्षा सम्झौतामा हस्ताक्षर गरेका छन्।

तेल धनी साउदी अरेबिया, आणविक शक्ति सम्पन्न पाकिस्तान र टर्की (जससँग नेटोको दोस्रो ठूलो सेना छ) ले शुक्रबार मक्कामा यो सम्झौता गरेका हुन्।

सम्झौतामा तीन देशमध्ये कुनै एकमाथि आक्रमण भएमा त्यसलाई तीनै देशमाथि आक्रमण मानिने उल्लेख छ। साउदी राजकुमार मोहम्मद बिन सलमान, टर्कीका राष्ट्रपति रजेप तैयप एर्दोगान र पाकिस्तानका प्रधानमन्त्री शेहबाज शरीफले मक्कामा यो सम्झौतामा हस्ताक्षर गरेका हुन्।

‘यो सम्झौता कुनै पनि आक्रमण विरुद्ध सामूहिक सुरक्षा बलियो बनाउनका लागि हो,’ पाकिस्तानको विदेश मन्त्रालयले भनेको छ।

यो सम्झौता यस्तो बेला भएको छ जब मध्यपूर्वमा तनाव बढेको छ र साउदी अरेबिया आफ्नो सुरक्षा साझेदार बढाउन खोजिरहेको छ।

अमेरिकी अधिकारीका अनुसार इरान र ओमानबिच होर्मुज जलमार्ग खोल्ने सम्झौता चाँडै हुन सक्छ। उनका अनुसार सम्झौता भएमा अमेरिका इरानी बन्दरगाहमाथिको नाकाबन्दी हटाउनेछ। तर इरानलाई जहाजबाट शुल्क लिन वा हस्तक्षेप गर्न दिने कुनै पनि शर्त अमेरिका स्वीकार गर्दैन।

इरान समर्थित हुथी समूहले शुक्रबार यमनको मारिब प्रान्तमा आक्रमण गरेको थियो। यसमा कम्तीमा दुई जनाको मृत्यु र १४ जना घाइते भए। हुथीले साउदी समर्थित सैन्य शिविरलाई निशाना बनाएको दाबी गरेको छ भने यमनी सरकारले शरणार्थी शिविर र आवासीय क्षेत्रमा आक्रमण भएको बताएको छ।

यसअघि बिहीबार साउदी अरेबियाको नजरान क्षेत्रमा पनि आक्रमण भएको थियो जसमा ११ जना घाइते भएका थिए। २०२२ को युद्धविरामपछि यमनमा लडाइँ रोकिएको थियो तर अहिले आक्रमण बढेको छ।

लेबनानी सेनाले शुक्रबार दक्षिणी गाउँ मन्सौरीमा बाटो खोल्ने क्रममा एक सैनिकलाई हल्का चोट लागेको बताएको छ। इजरायली ड्रोनले बुलडोजरमा आक्रमण गरेको थियो। इजरायलले यसबारे कुनै टिप्पणी गरेको छैन। एजेन्सी

articles.title: नेपालमा एक वर्षमै ६१ हजारभन्दा बढी मुद्दा, औसतमा दैनिक १६७ अपराध दर्ता
articles.summary:
नेपालमा एक वर्षको अवधिमा ६१ हजारभन्दा बढी आपराधिक मुद्दा दर्ता भएका छन् ।

नेपाल प्रहरीले आर्थिक वर्ष २०८२/८३ को वार्षिक कार्यप्रगति विवरण सार्वजनिक गर्दै एक वर्षमा कुल ६१ हजार १६ वटा मुद्दा दर्ता भएको जनाएको हो । प्रहरीका अनुसार यो संख्या अघिल्लो आर्थिक वर्षको तुलनामा बढेको हो। आर्थिक वर्ष २०८१/८२ मा ५८ हजार ४७२ मुद्दा दर्ता भएकोमा २०८२/८३ मा यो संख्या बढेर ६१ हजार १६ पुगेको छ।

प्रहरीको तथ्यांकअनुसार औसतमा दैनिक १६७ वटा मुद्दा दर्ता हुने गरेको छ। सबैभन्दा धेरै मुद्दा बैंकिङ कसुरतर्फ देखिएको छ। एक वर्षमा बैंकिङ कसुरका १२ हजार ९५० मुद्दा दर्ता भएका छन्। त्यसपछि सार्वजनिक हित, स्वास्थ्य, सुरक्षा, सुविधा र नैतिकताविरुद्धका ८ हजार ७०७ कसुर दर्ता भएका छन्।

आत्महत्यासम्बन्धी घटना ६ हजार १९७, लागूऔषधसम्बन्धी ५ हजार ७९१ र साधारण चोरीका ३ हजार ५२४ मुद्दा दर्ता भएका छन्। जबरजस्ती करणीका २ हजार ३८०, ठगी, आपराधिक विश्वासघात तथा आपराधिक लाभसम्बन्धी २ हजार ३७५ र सवारी ज्यानसम्बन्धी २ हजार ९४ मुद्दा दर्ता भएका छन्।

प्रहरीको विवरणले नेपालमा अपराधको प्रकृति परम्परागत चोरी, हिंसा र अन्य अपराधसँगै आर्थिक तथा लागूऔषधजन्य कसुरतर्फ पनि गम्भीर चुनौती देखाइरहेको संकेत गरेको छ। प्रदेशगत रूपमा काठमाडौं उपत्यकामा सबैभन्दा धेरै १५ हजार २९७ मुद्दा दर्ता भएका छन्। मधेशमा १० हजार ७५० र कोशीमा ९ हजार ८६३ मुद्दा दर्ता भएका छन्।

articles.title: देश धान्ने क्षेत्रमै संकट, श्रमिक विदेश पठाउन बन्द !
articles.summary:
काठमाडौं । वैदेशिक रोजगारीबाट आउने रेमिट्यान्सले देशको अर्थतन्त्र धान्न सहयोग पु¥याइरहेका म्यानपावर व्यवसायीले सरकारविरुद्ध दबाब बढाएका छन् । १५ बुँदे माग अघि सार्दै नेपाल वैदेशिक रोजगार व्यवसायी संघले शुक्रवारदेखि वैदेशिक रोजगारीमा श्रमिक पठाउने सम्पूर्ण प्रक्रिया बन्द गर्ने घोषणा गरेको छ । व्यवसायीहरूले नीतिगत सुधार नभएसम्म कामदार नपठाउने अडान लिएका छन् ।

नेपाल वैदेशिक रोजगार व्यवसायी संघले वैदेशिक रोजगार क्षेत्रका नीतिगत समस्या समाधान नभएको भन्दै शुक्रवारदेखि श्रमिक विदेश पठाउने कार्य पूर्ण रूपमा स्थगित गरेको छ । काठमाडौँमा पत्रकार सम्मेलन गर्दै संघले रेमिट्यान्सले मुलुकको अर्थतन्त्रमा ठूलो योगदान पु¥याए पनि सरकारले समयानुकूल नीति सुधार नगर्दा व्यवसायी र श्रमिक दुवै प्रभावित भएको जनाएको छ ।

संघले वैदेशिक रोजगार ऐन–२०६४ लाई समयसापेक्ष संशोधन, पारदर्शी लागत निर्धारण, वैज्ञानिक सेवा शुल्क, श्रमिक लक्षित गन्तव्य मुलुकको हवाई भाडा घटाउने तथा कृत्रिम अभाव अन्त्य गर्न माग गरेको छ । युरोपका नयाँ श्रम बजार, दक्षिण कोरियाको ई–सेभेन भिसा, जापानको ईएसडी कार्यक्रम सञ्चालन, महिला घरेलु कामदारका लागि नयाँ गन्तव्य खुला गर्ने र विभिन्न मुलुकमा देखिएका प्रशासनिक तथा बिचौलिया समस्या कूटनीतिक पहलमार्फत समाधान गर्नुपर्ने माग पनि अघि सारिएको छ ।

संघले मागपत्र प्रमाणीकरण र श्रम स्वीकृतिलाई पूर्ण रूपमा स्वचालित बनाउन, ५ हजारभन्दा बढी नेपाली श्रमिक रहेका मुलुकमा श्रम सहचारी तथा काउन्सिलर नियुक्त गर्न, व्यवसायीले राखेको धरौटीको ब्याज उपलब्ध गराउन र श्रमिकलाई बिना धितो सहुलियतपूर्ण कर्जा दिने व्यवस्था गर्न पनि सरकारसँग माग गरेको छ । अध्यक्ष खत्रीले विशेष परिस्थितिमा सरकारकै निर्णय कार्यान्वयन गर्दा व्यवसायीमाथि कारबाही गरिएको आरोप लगाउँदै अब नीतिगत सुधार नभएसम्म श्रमिक नपठाउने स्पष्ट चेतावनी दिएका छन् ।

संघले आफ्ना सबै माग सम्बोधन नभएसम्म शून्य समय घोषणा गर्दै वैदेशिक रोजगारीमा श्रमिक पठाउने सम्पूर्ण प्रक्रिया बन्द रहने जनाएको छ । व्यवसायीहरूको यो निर्णयले वैदेशिक रोजगारीमा जान तयारी गरिरहेका हजारौं नेपाली श्रमिक प्रत्यक्ष प्रभावित हुने देखिएको छ ।

articles.title: सेती नदि थुनिएर ताल बन्यो, स्थानीय जाग्राम बस्न बाध्य
articles.summary:
कास्की । केहि दिन यताको निरन्तर वर्षाले पोखराको रामघाटमा सेती नदी थुनिएर विशाल ताल बनेको छ । जसका कारण नदिसँगै जोडिएका सुकुम्बासी बस्ती बाढीले बगाउने जोखिममा रहेका छन् ।

सेती नदीलाई लिएर पोखराको भौगोलिक बनावट अत्यन्त जोखिममा रहेको चर्चा गरिन्छ , तर सेतिले निम्त्याएको जोखिम न्यून गर्न भने कुनै निकायको ध्यान पुग्न सकेको छैन । झट्ट हेर्दा यो दृश्य कुनै तालको होला भन्ने लाग्न सक्छ, तर नझुक्किनुस् यो कुनै ताल भने होइन ।

केहीदिन यता निरन्तर परेको वर्षको कारण सेती नदीमा पानीको बहाव निकै उच्च छ । हो पोखरा रामघाटमा फराकिलो रहेको सेती नदीको निकास सानो हुँदा पानी जान नसकेर विशाल ताल नै बनेको छ । सेती नदी थुनिएर ताल बन्दा अहिलेसम्म क्षति त भएको छैन तर संभावित क्षतिको जोखिम भने निकै बढेको छ ।

दाह संस्कारका लागि बनाइएका घाटहरु पुरै जलमग्न बनेका छन् । सेती किनारसँगै दुई दर्जन बढी सुकुम्बासी बस्ती छ, बर्खा लागे पछि कतिबेला बाढीले बगाउने हो भनेर जाग्राम बस्नु पर्ने अवस्था छ । अहिले ३ वर्ष यताकै ठूलो र डरलाग्दो तरिकाले सेती बढेको स्थानीय बताउँछन् ।

सेती नदी पोखराको अधिकांस भागमा भूमिगत भएर बगेको छ । पोखराको बीच भाग अर्थात् रामघाटमा भने सेती सतहमा देखिन्छ । यस आसपासको क्षेत्र अत्यन्त जोखिममा रहेपनि सुकुम्बासीका नाममा बस्ती बस्ने क्रम भने नरोकिदो जोखिम झनै बढ्दैछ । पछिल्लो समय झनझन गहिरिदै गएको सेती खोंच र निरन्तरको बर्षाका कारण कतिबेला ठूलो दुर्घटना निम्तिने भन्ने इतिहासविद्को चिन्ता छ ।

पोखराको भू–बनोट र निरन्तर वर्षाले भासिन सक्ने सम्भाव्यताले पोखरालाई वर्षेनी जोखिम तर्फ धकेलेको भूगोलविद्को बुझाई छ । नदी थुनिएर आफ्नो गतिमा जान नपाउँदा निरन्तर जमिनलाई खियाउनाले जोखिम बढेको भूगोलविद् कृष्ण प्रसाद पौडेल बताउँछन् ।

पोखराको भू–बनोट, बेलाबेलामा भएका जमीन भासिने घटना र भूमिगतरूपमा बगेको सेतीका कारण पोखराको जोखिमबारे बेलाबेला चर्चा हुने गर्दछ, तर त्यो चर्चालाई दीर्घकालीन समाधानको बाटोतर्फ भने कुनै निकायले लैजान सकेका छैनन् ।

articles.title: स्तनपान प्रवद्र्धनमा जोड, दोलखामा स्वास्थ्य सचेतना
articles.summary:
दोलखा । जीवनको दिगो सुरुवातका लागि स्तनपान प्रभावकारी कार्यहरूको सुदृढीकरण“ भन्ने नारासहित दोलखाको भीमेश्वर नगरपालिका–५ स्थित माटी स्वास्थ्य चौकीमा विश्व स्तनपान सप्ताह–२०२६ मनाइएको छ । कार्यक्रममा गर्भवती तथा सुत्केरी आमाहरूलाई स्वास्थ्य सेवा, पोषण सामग्री वितरण तथा महिला स्वास्थ्य स्वयंसेविकालाई प्रोत्साहन गरिएको छ ।

विश्व स्तनपान सप्ताह–२०२६ को अवसरमा दोलखामा आयोजित कार्यक्रममा धुलिखेल अस्पताल दोलखाका विशेषज्ञ चिकित्सकहरूले गर्भवती महिलाको स्वास्थ्य परीक्षण, अल्ट्रासाउन्ड, स्वास्थ्य परामर्श तथा स्तनपान र शिशु पोषणबारे अभिमुखीकरण गरेका छन् ।

कार्यक्रममा गर्भवती तथा सुत्केरी आमालाई पोषण सामग्री, ब्ल्यांकेट तथा महिला स्वास्थ्य स्वयंसेविका र माटी स्वास्थ्य चौकीका स्वास्थ्यकर्मीलाई छाता वितरण गरिएको छ । ती सामग्री पूर्व स्वास्थ्य चौकी प्रमुख रामकृष्ण मास्केको पहलमा विभिन्न दाताबाट संकलन गरिएको हो ।

कार्यक्रममा जिल्लाको स्वास्थ्य अवस्था, शिशु स्वास्थ्यमा आमाको दूधको महत्व र स्तनपान प्रवद्र्धन अभियानबारे जानकारी गराइएको छ । समुदायस्तरमा यस्ता कार्यक्रमलाई निरन्तरता दिनुपर्नेमा जोड दिइएको छ ।

भीमेश्वर नगरपालिकाले मातृ तथा शिशु स्वास्थ्यलाई प्राथमिकतामा राख्दै स्वास्थ्य संस्थासँगको सहकार्यलाई थप प्रभावकारी बनाउने जनाएको छ ।

नेपाल क्षयरोग निवारण संस्थाले समुदायमा स्वास्थ्य सचेतना अभिवृद्धिका कार्यक्रमलाई निरन्तरता दिइने जनाएको छ ।

कार्यक्रममा गर्भवती तथा सुत्केरी आमाहरूलाई स्वास्थ्य सेवा, पोषण सामग्री वितरण तथा स्वास्थ्य स्वयंसेविका र स्वास्थ्यकर्मीलाई सम्मान गर्दै स्तनपानको महत्व समुदायसम्म पु¥याउने प्रयास गरिएको आयोजकले जनाएको छ ।

articles.title: Concerns grow over foreign employment as Nepali agencies halt process
articles.summary:
The Nepal Association of Foreign Employment Agencies has halted the process for Nepalis’ labour migration starting Friday, pressing the government to address its demands.

The 15-point charter seeks the withdrawal of disciplinary action against 771 manpower companies and the introduction of a scientific service fee structure, among other demands.

The association made the announcement after the 15-day ultimatum it had issued to the Ministry of Youth, Labour and Employment ended without the government addressing the concerns.

The Department of Foreign Employment had taken action against hundreds of recruitment agencies for allegedly charging workers fees beyond the government-set ceiling, sending workers to destination countries through Indian airports without approval, and failing to employ workers in destination countries according to contract agreements.

Association officials have warned that member agencies will not participate in the institutional labour approval process for sending workers abroad until their demands are addressed.

The decision to halt the deployment of migrant workers will affect hundreds of thousands of Nepali youths who rely on labour markets in the Gulf countries, Malaysia, and parts of Europe for employment opportunities and a better future. The move will also affect remittance inflows, a major contributor to Nepal’s economy, with annual receipts equivalent to around a third of the country’s gross development product.

Dik Bahadur Khatri (Kumar), president of the association, said that although foreign employment has become one of the major pillars of Nepal’s economy, the sector is facing a crisis due to policy inconsistencies, impractical regulations and a lack of timely reforms. The number of workers receiving new labour approvals declined by 99,553 last fiscal year compared to the previous year, a drop of 19.7 percent.

“Since 1993-94, the foreign employment sector has brought in large amounts of remittances, helping keep the economy afloat. It has boosted foreign currency reserves and contributed to reducing the trade deficit. Around 64 percent of Nepali households are directly or indirectly linked to this sector,” Khatri said. “However, practical policies have never been introduced to properly manage it.”

The agencies have called for amendments to the Foreign Employment Act, 2007, arguing that the government should introduce a transparent service fee structure based on the actual costs involved in recruiting workers. They said the current “free visa, free ticket” policy is impractical to implement and that the absence of a clear fee mechanism has encouraged informal transactions and complicated business operations.

Of the 406,404 Nepali workers who received new labour approvals and went abroad for employment last fiscal year, 268,990—or around 66 percent—processed through manpower companies. Around 31.6 percent made individual arrangements, while only about 2 percent used government channels for migration.

The association has also demanded intervention to control airfares to labour destinations, prevent artificial shortages and simplify the verification of demand letters from new destination countries. It has called for improved access to labour markets in European countries, South Korea under the E-9 system, Japan through the Specified Skilled Worker programme, and better management of foreign employment opportunities for female domestic workers.

The group has sought worker-friendly labour agreements with destination countries, separate mechanisms to handle institutional and individual complaints, and full automation of demand letter verification, pre-labour approval and final labour approval processes.

The agencies have also urged the government to use diplomatic channels to address what they described as monopolistic practices in worker recruitment in various countries. They have opposed requirements such as Saudi Arabia’s Skill Verification Programme and biometric system, the UAE’s police certificate verification process, and recruitment-related monopolies in Malaysia.

The association has demanded the appointment of labour attachés and labour counsellors in countries with more than 5,000 Nepali workers, a halt to issuing new manpower licences, and the issuance of new licences only when required based on clear standards.

It has also sought the return of interest earned on cash deposits maintained by foreign employment agencies, stricter action against illegal transactions and excessive interest lending, and access to collateral-free or subsidised loans for migrant workers through banks and financial institutions.

The ministry has urged recruitment agencies to follow established procedures. “The ministry is working internally on determining the service fee. A draft amendment to the Foreign Employment Act has already been prepared to address issues requiring legal changes and has been sent for inter-ministerial consultations before finalisation,” said Pitambar Ghimire, spokesperson for the ministry. “We are committed to improving the labour sector.”

If the suspension continues for an extended period, thousands of workers who have already received labour approvals and are preparing to leave for jobs abroad could be affected.

Stakeholders say any disruption in foreign employment could have wider economic consequences, as remittances remain a major source of foreign exchange for Nepal. Nepal received Rs2.12 trillion in remittances in the first 11 months of the last fiscal year, a 38.2 percent increase compared to the same period a year earlier, according to the Nepal Rastra Bank.

The Joint Trade Union Coordination Centre, the umbrella body of Nepal’s trade unions, has opposed any service fee arrangement that increases the financial burden on workers.

“The government should not retreat from determining service fees because of the manpower agencies’ protest. We do not accept a policy that places recruitment costs and service fees on workers,” said Binod Shrestha, chairperson of the coordination centre.

“All costs related to worker recruitment should be borne by employers. If manpower companies stop sending workers, the government should explore alternatives, including using state mechanisms.”

Shrestha said foreign employment that forces workers to take high-interest loans is unsustainable. “If workers have to carry a debt burden just to get employment and spend years repaying it, such employment cannot be considered beneficial,” he said. “We need quality jobs, and the government should focus on creating such opportunities within Nepal.”

articles.title: Thapathali hospital cuts neonatal deaths by over two-thirds in five years
articles.summary:
Neonatal deaths at the Paropakar Maternity and Women’s Hospital, Thapathali have fallen by more than two-thirds over the last five years, thanks to a series of measures the hospital has implemented to improve newborn care.

According to the hospital administration, neonatal deaths at the hospital stood at around eight per 1,000 live births five years ago. The number has now declined to around 2.5 percent.

“Due to various preventive measures taken by our hospital administration, we have been successful in reducing newborn deaths,” said Dr Shree Prasad Adhikari, director of the hospital. “Our success shows that neonatal deaths can be reduced further and there is still room for improvement.”

Neonatal means the first 28 days of a baby’s life. More than 2,000 neonates are estimated to die every year in Nepal.

A recent Nepal Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey carried out by the National Statistics Office in partnership with UNICEF shows that neonatal deaths are still 17 per 1,000 live births.

According to data provided by the Health Information Management System under the Department of Health Services, 2,630 perinatal deaths were recorded in 130 hospitals of 57 districts in the fiscal year 2025-026.

Officials acknowledge that the actual number of perinatal and neonatal deaths could be much higher, as the data covers only hospitals with the Maternal and Perinatal Death Surveillance and Response programme.

Maternal and child health experts say multiple factors — infection, birth asphyxia, premature birth, hypothermia, low birth weight, poor maternal health during pregnancy, inadequate postnatal care, and a shortage of trained human resources — are responsible for the country’s high perinatal and neonatal deaths.

“We have taken various measures to reduce neonatal deaths in our hospital, including appointing additional doctors and nurses, introducing newborn screening and treatment, improving the management of birth asphyxia, hypothermia, strengthening infection control, and replacing formula milk with mother’s milk,” Adhikari said. “Eight deaths per 1,000 live births at the central hospital were alarming. We have reduced the number to 2.5, but even that is still high.”

More than 24,000 women give birth at the Thapathali hospital every year.

Doctors said that, in the past, a nurse had to look after 10 sick newborns admitted to the neonatal intensive care unit. Now, one trained nurse looks after only three babies.

“In developed countries, one nurse provides care to one patient in intensive care, but we cannot afford that level of staffing,” said Dr Sailendra Bir Karmacharya, a senior consultant paediatrician at the hospital. “The number of trained doctors and nurses has increased in recent years, and this has helped prevent avoidable newborn deaths.”

Previously, many newborns developed bloating and intestinal infections after being fed formula milk. But since the hospital established a human milk bank, such infections and related complications have declined markedly, Karmachary said.

The hospital has also improved hygiene standards and introduced a newborn screening programme, enabling healthcare providers to identify health risks early and begin treatment promptly.

Instead of formula milk, preterm and low-birth-weight babies are now fed their mothers’ milk, which reduces the risk of infections and improves their chances of survival, according to Karmacharya.

One of the Sustainable Development Goals is to reduce neonatal mortality to 12 per 1,000 live births by 2030.

The SDGs, a follow-up on the Millennium Development Goals (MDGs), aim to end poverty, hunger, and all forms of inequality in the world by 2030.

articles.title: Pitch overhaul in progress for NPL and U19 World Cup
articles.summary:
Madhu Tamang dug his thumbs into the black clay, feeling for roots on the pitches at the Tribhuvan University International Cricket Ground in Kirtipur on Friday morning.

Around Tamang, ground staff stripped away topsoil—scraping the pitch down to its foundation to yank out dead vegetation before transplanting fresh local grass taken from inside the 30-yard circle.

“Ground staff have removed the ruined soil all the way down to the roots while preparing the new pitch, after which they started planting grass, which will be completed today,” said Roshan Kumar Singh, vice president of the Cricket Association of Nepal (CAN) and tournament coordinator for the U19 World Cup preparations.

For two years, this strip of dirt has held a dirty secret in Nepali cricket.

When the previous season of the NPL kicked off, franchise scouts built rosters around pace because Kirtipur’s pitches were laid with fresh green grass. Teams anticipated a permanent shift in surface behaviour—one that would offer genuine carry for pacers alongside traditional spin.

Early on, it delivered. Sudurpaschim Royals’ Scott Kuggeleijn, Chitwan Rhinos’ Sohail Tanvir and Rijan Dhakal, Janakpur Bolts’ Kishor Mahato, and Kathmandu Gorkhas’ Karan KC found immediate success.

But the seam movement was short-lived. Within a week, the grass withered, and the pitch reverted to its low, slow nature. Spinners like Janakpur’s Lalit Narayan Rajbanshi, Karnali Yaks’ Bipin Sharma, and Sudurpaschim’s Saif Zaib dominated the remainder of the tournament.

While the TU Ground itself has gradually transformed into a modern international facility with grandstands and floodlights, the pitch characteristics have remained unchanged. Now, CAN is undertaking a major pitch overhaul across three venues ahead of the upcoming NPL third edition and the 16-nation ICC U19 Women’s T20 World Cup—the largest cricket event Nepal has co-hosted with Bangladesh.

Grass laying at Kirtipur was completed on Friday, following earlier work at Upper Mulpani, while work at Lower Mulpani remains ongoing. In total, eight pitches are being constructed in Kirtipur, seven in Upper Mulpani, and six in Lower Mulpani.

“The crucial factor is how long the grass remains on the wicket. As long as the grass stays, the pitch remains good. Once it dies off, the surface turns flat,” Singh explained. “If grass roots penetrate four inches deep, they bind the soil together, allowing the wicket to set properly.”

Achieving that four-inch depth typically requires four months. However, curators have barely two and a half months before the NPL returns after Dashain. Furthermore, as the month of Bhadra begins, root growth naturally slows.

“Given the tight timeframe, the chances of roots reaching the full four inches are slim,” Singh admitted. “Had we used Bermuda grass, the wicket would have lasted for years, but we simply did not have the lead time. Still, we are confident it will perform well.”

CAN is also leaning on the weather. Because deep moisture encourages root penetration, a prolonged monsoon could work in their favour despite the delayed start.

"If the monsoon stretches out, it will actually help," Singh noted. "We expect grass to hold on the wicket for about two weeks into the NPL. After that, based on past behavior, the pitch will likely turn flat again."

The entire pitch renovation across Kirtipur and Mulpani is estimated at Rs7 to 8 million—excluding major infrastructure—funded upfront by CAN and subject to reimbursement by the ICC.

While TU Ground will be the primary host for the NPL, all three venues will serve the U19 World Cup, with Lower Mulpani accommodating 5,000 fans and Upper Mulpani adding a 2,000-seat temporary stand. Curators Prafulla Pradhan and Bangladesh’s Mohammad Abdul Al Mamun are overseeing operations at Mulpani.

“Once the playing surfaces are finalised, full facility upgrades will commence at Kirtipur—including renovated dressing rooms, ice baths, dining halls, VIP boxes, numbered seating, and streamlined entry gates,” Singh said. “Security remains a top priority, and comprehensive protocols will be locked in once ICC representatives arrive.”

For CAN and its groundskeepers, the coming weeks will reveal whether time and weather are on their side—or if Kirtipur’s turf will once again have the final say.

articles.title: Sarlahi farmers finally home, but the fertiliser crisis remains
articles.summary:
Two Nepali brothers who spent 38 days in an Indian jail after being arrested while carrying fertiliser home for their farm have been released on bail, bringing an end to a weeks-long legal ordeal that has drawn attention to Nepal's chronic fertiliser shortages.

Suresh Prasad Singh, 55, and his elder brother Nagendra Prasad Singh, 60, of ward 5 of Balara Municipality in Sarlahi district were freed on Friday, two days after an Indian court granted them bail.

The brothers had crossed into the Indian border town of Sonbarsa on July 1 to buy fertiliser after failing to obtain it in Nepal during the peak paddy planting season.

Like many farmers across Nepal's southern plains, they had struggled to secure subsidised chemical fertiliser as the monsoon planting season got underway. With no fertiliser available locally and fearing their rice crop would fail, they decided to make the short trip across the border.

On their way back, carrying two sacks of urea and six sacks of diammonium phosphate (DAP) on bicycles, they were stopped by a joint team from India's Sashastra Seema Bal (SSB) and the agriculture department.

Indian authorities accused them of illegally transporting fertiliser across the border and charged them with fertiliser smuggling. They were first taken to Sonbarsa police station before being transferred to Dumra Jail in Sitamarhi district, where they remained in custody for 38 days.

For the two brothers, who had crossed the border simply to save their rice crop, the experience became one of the most traumatic episodes of their lives.

The ordeal of 38 days behind bars was visible on the brothers' faces after their release.

"It was something I never imagined," Nagendra said. "I ended up in prison in another country. It was an extremely painful experience."

He described the 38 days behind bars as feeling like "living through another lifetime."

On Wednesday, a single bench of Principal District and Sessions Judge, Akhilesh Kumar Jha, of the Dumra Civil Court in Sitamarhi district ordered the brothers' release on bail.

Although the court granted bail immediately, procedural formalities delayed their release.

The bail order was forwarded to Dumra Jail on Thursday after court officials completed the paperwork. The brothers signed the required documents inside the prison before being taken back to the court, where the bail process was formally completed.

Their lawyer, Sanjay Kumar Jha, said the brothers were released only after relatives pledged family land as bail bonds.

Under Indian law, local guarantors were required for bail.

Two Indian citizens, Tapeshwar Singh and Baleshwar Singh, both relatives of the family through marriage, stood surety for the brothers by mortgaging land worth 10,000 Indian rupees each.

The brothers must now appear before the Indian court every month until their case is resolved. Failure to attend could result in legal consequences for their guarantors, another lawyer representing them, Kiran Kumar Chaudhary, said.

Their arrest has highlighted a problem that returns almost every year in Nepal's southern border districts: chronic shortages of chemical fertiliser during the most critical stages of the farming season.

Unable to obtain fertiliser through official distribution channels, the brothers travelled across the border, hoping to secure enough supplies for their own fields.

Instead, they found themselves facing criminal charges in a foreign country.

"A small effort to save my own crop turned into legal and psychological suffering," Suresh said.

Back home, the prolonged detention placed heavy emotional and financial strain on the family.

Suresh's son, Abhishek Singh, said the family had struggled in the absence of its two senior members.

"When the heads of the family are suddenly gone, it's impossible to describe what life becomes," he said. "My father and uncle have finally been released after a long wait. We have learned a painful lesson. Our ordeal should serve as a wake-up call for the Nepal government."

The family said they still have not been able to obtain fertiliser in Nepal.

Their release was delayed repeatedly because of the Indian court process.

Abhishek had filed a petition seeking an early hearing on July 24, but the hearing was postponed thrice after the chief judge went on leave.

The brothers finally secured bail on August 5 after lawyers Sanjay Kumar Jha and Kiran Chaudhary argued that they were ordinary Nepali farmers, not fertiliser smugglers.

Even after the bail order was issued, another obstacle emerged.

Indian law required local citizens to act as guarantors, leaving the family scrambling for someone eligible to meet the legal requirement. Their release became possible only after relatives living in India agreed to stand surety.

Former lawmaker Dev Prasad Timilsina said the case has once again exposed the hardships routinely faced by farmers in Nepal's Madhesh Province and elsewhere in the country.

"Every year the government promises to support agriculture and subsidise fertiliser," he said. "Yet when farmers need fertiliser the most, during planting or weeding season, they cannot get it."

He said the brothers' release had brought relief to their family, but their ordeal reflected the reality faced by hundreds of thousands of Nepali farmers.

"So long as the state fails to establish a reliable system that provides farmers with seeds and fertiliser on time, more farmers trying simply to save their crops will continue to face unnecessary hardship and even criminal punishment along the border," Timilsina said.

Kantipur was the first to report on the arrest of the Singh brothers. Following the report, Foreign Minister Shisir Khanal took up the matter and began diplomatic coordination with the Indian government through Nepal’s embassy in New Delhi. However, their release was delayed because of the court process. Khanal said the delay was due to legal procedures in India.

Nepal faces severe shortages of chemical fertiliser almost every year during the peak farming season. Because the government has repeatedly failed to ensure adequate and timely supplies, farmers in border areas have been forced to depend on Indian markets to protect their livelihoods and crops.

Although many farmers cross the border only to buy small quantities of fertiliser for their own fields rather than for commercial purposes, Indian security agencies have taken a much stricter approach this year. Increased border surveillance and tougher enforcement have added to the difficulties faced by farmers in the region.

Farmers say the problem begins within the country, where local allocations are far below actual demand and distribution systems lack transparency, preventing fertiliser from reaching smallholders.

Manoj Mehta, ward 5 chair of Balara Municipality, where the Singh brothers live, said the ward needs around 2,000 sacks of urea during the farming season but received only 40 sacks.

“How can we distribute such a small quantity among farmers? When there is no fertiliser available, farmers have no option but to cross the border,” he said. “If they go to India, they are accused of smuggling. In Nepal, the fertiliser is unavailable. When will this problem facing farmers finally be solved?”

The Singh brothers are residents of his ward.

For years, farmers living along the border have travelled to Indian markets early in the morning by bicycle or motorcycle to buy one or two sacks of fertiliser for personal agricultural use.

But recent restrictions by Indian security personnel have made that increasingly difficult, said Mohammad Asim, a farmer from Jingdawa in Paroha Municipality.

“In previous years, when farmers carried small quantities of fertiliser for household use, the Sashastra Seema Bal personnel would usually allow them through after brief questioning or with some flexibility,” he said. “This year, the situation is completely different. They are now quick to label farmers as smugglers.”

The arrest of the Singh brothers, who spent weeks in Sitamarhi jail after being caught carrying urea and DAP fertiliser intended for their own fields, has created fear among farmers living in Nepal’s border districts.

Indian authorities say the crackdown is linked to restrictions on the export of subsidised fertiliser provided by the Indian government to its own farmers. Because such fertiliser cannot legally be taken out of India without permission, the SSB has been treating even small quantities carried by Nepali farmers as illegal exports, leading to arrests and criminal proceedings.

Under India’s Fertiliser (Control) Order (FCO), introduced to regulate the price, quality and supply of fertiliser, agricultural fertilisers are classified as subsidised commodities distributed to farmers. The rules prohibit their export outside India without authorisation, particularly for commercial purposes.

Citing these regulations, Indian security officials have tightened controls along the Nepal border in recent years. Farmers say even a single sack of fertiliser is now being stopped from entering Nepal.

The restrictions come at a critical time for Nepali farmers, as paddy transplantation has ended and fields require fertiliser application. Yet many farmers say they are still unable to obtain the supplies they need.

articles.title: Exhibit review: In ‘Dialogue and Perception’, colour does all the talking
articles.summary:
Some exhibitions ask viewers to search for meaning. Others ask them to surrender to feeling first. Sagar Manandhar’s latest exhibition ‘Dialogue and Perception (Sambad ra Dristikon)’ belongs firmly to the latter.

Stepping into the Kala Salon, what strikes first is not the subject matter but the remarkable harmony of colour. Every painting appears to revolve around a dominant hue, allowing secondary colours to grow organically around it. The canvases are saturated with vivid blues, oranges, yellows and purples, yet they never descend into visual noise. Instead, the colours settle into an unexpected balance, creating works that feel energetic without becoming chaotic.

The exhibition is unmistakably abstract, but abstraction here never feels directionless. Strong geometric forms anchor each composition while carefully maintained lines provide structure beneath the apparent spontaneity. There is discipline behind every gesture. Thin borders often frame the compositions, suggesting restraint, yet somewhere within each work a section seems determined to escape those boundaries, pushing outward as though the painting itself refuses confinement.

Walking through the exhibit, one begins to recognise a distinct visual language. Certain rhythmic squiggles recur throughout the paintings, resembling sound frequencies frozen into colour. They weave across the canvas like vibrations made visible, hinting that the artist experiences the world less through objects than through resonance. Even the sequencing of the paintings within the gallery feels intentional, almost as if viewers are moving through different movements of a musical composition.

It is difficult to mistake these paintings for anyone else’s. Despite experimenting with new techniques and materials, Manandhar has developed a recognisable signature. His brushwork, layered acrylic lines and rhythmic mark-making create a consistency that ties the exhibition together while still allowing individual works to explore different emotional territories.

Texture plays an equally important role. Paint bubbles emerge from the surface, thick acrylic ridges catch the light, while scratched lines and raised forms introduce a physicality that photographs cannot fully capture. In many works, the surface itself becomes part of the narrative. The acrylic seems alive, refusing to remain a passive medium.

Manandhar reinforces this relationship with material through his process. Rather than treating paint as something secondary to the final image, he describes acrylic as carrying emotion in itself. He speaks less about controlling an outcome than about trusting the process, allowing meanings to reveal themselves as he works. His abstraction is therefore not an attempt to conceal meaning but to discover it.

That philosophy becomes evident throughout the exhibition. These paintings do not feel planned in the conventional sense. Instead, they resemble emotional snapshots—moments where feeling has been translated into colour before language has the chance to intervene. There is something strangely nostalgic about them. Although entirely abstract, many of the works evoke the sensation of childhood, when the world seemed impossibly bright and uncomplicated. They feel less like representations of memory than the emotions memory leaves behind.

His understanding of colour further distinguishes the exhibition. Manandhar repeatedly places complementary colours alongside one another—blue against orange, yellow against purple—allowing contrasts to generate unexpected harmony. Colours that conventionally appear incompatible somehow coexist effortlessly under his hand. Small droplets of paint occasionally interrupt otherwise cohesive surfaces, momentarily pulling attention away from the composition before eventually folding back into it. Even these interruptions seem deliberate, preventing the eye from settling too comfortably.

Gradients soften transitions between otherwise bold passages, while the combination of acrylic paint and marker creates subtle shifts in texture and line quality. One senses an artist continually testing what his chosen medium is capable of.

Perhaps the exhibition's most compelling idea lies in Manandhar's relationship with sound. He speaks of having a special connection with auditory experience, something that manifests visually through repeated rhythmic forms and textured surfaces. Different scratches and lines remind him of different sounds produced by various materials. His experiments extend beyond canvas altogether.

Recent works include acrylic sheets that are allowed to dry into independent surfaces, as well as glass engravings that resonate like singing bowls when struck. These material explorations challenge the expectation that painting must remain confined to stretched canvas.

Interestingly, Manandhar says he sees paintings through palettes rather than individual colours. Rather than asking what blue or red symbolises, he considers what an entire palette feels like. This perspective explains one of the exhibition’s most intriguing inversions. While red is traditionally associated with anger, passion or heat, Manandhar instinctively reaches for blue. Likewise, sadness or emotional heaviness often emerges through reds instead of blues. The emotional vocabulary is deliberately reversed, forcing viewers to question their own assumptions about colour symbolism.

His influences also reveal themselves subtly. Manandhar credits his father, veteran artist Kiran Manandhar, as his greatest inspiration, particularly admiring his discipline and enduring creative energy. He also speaks of his appreciation for Buddha Nepali’s illusionistic abstraction. Yet despite these influences, the work never feels derivative. It remains distinctly his own.

The exhibition is not without moments of unevenness. Some experiments, particularly the detached acrylic surfaces, still feel exploratory rather than fully resolved. Similarly, a handful of colour droplets appear visually disconnected from the surrounding compositions, momentarily interrupting rather than enriching the rhythm.

Yet these minor imperfections seem inseparable from the exhibition’s central philosophy of experimentation. Manandhar is clearly less interested in polished certainty than in discovering what paint can become.

There is a temptation when viewing abstract art to search immediately for familiar forms—a landscape, a face or a tree. Manandhar acknowledges this instinct himself, observing that people naturally cling to what they already recognise. His paintings gently resist that impulse. Instead of offering identifiable subjects, they invite viewers to experience movement, rhythm, texture and colour before interpretation.

By the end of the exhibition, the paintings begin to feel less like images than recordings. They capture fleeting emotional frequencies that exist somewhere between sound, colour and memory.

‘Dialogue and Perception’ is an apt title because neither exists independently in Manandhar's work. The conversation begins with paint and canvas, but it doesn't end there. It continues between colour and sound, artist and viewer, certainty and imagination. His paintings ask for neither agreement nor interpretation. They ask only that we look– and perhaps, if we stay long enough, learn to listen.

____________________________________

Dialogue And Perception (Sambad ra Dristikon)

Where: The Kala Salon, Thamel

Time: 11:00 am to 8:00 pm

Entry: Free

articles.title: Book review: The nurse who chose Jumla over the world
articles.summary:
Radha Paudel’s Madan Puraskar-winning ‘Attack on Khalanga’ has been out for 13 years now. The English translation itself, ‘Jumla: A Nurse's Story’, is coming up on a decade of being on the shelves.

The book recounts Paudel’s experiences leading up to, during and after the Maoist attack on Khalanga, Jumla’s district headquarters. It is a record of the poverty- and misery-filled lives of the everyday people of Jumla. There are striking examples of this misery in the book. For example, in one part, Paudel offers a bar of soap to a lady washing herself by the river. The lady begins to bleed from her hands after she uses the soap, her skin not used to it.

The book is also about the Nepali Civil War. Paudel shares such extensive details of the Maoist attack on Khalanga that one can picture what it might have been like.

But along with these two popular ideas about what the story is about, there is another increasingly relevant one—that of migration in the author’s case but also generally of immigration.

It is through listening to her father’s stories of Jumla when she was a child that Paudel grows curious about the place. He often used to tell her, she writes, that she should return to Jumla as an adult to do what she can to help the people of the district. Paudel herself grew up in poverty, but whenever she brought it up as a child, her father used to tell her that they may be poor, but poorer still were the people of Jumla.

The author does well for herself. After completing an undergraduate nursing degree, she goes on to get her master’s in public health. And when all of her friends from nursing school move to the cities and sometimes abroad, like to the United Kingdom, Paudel moves to Jumla.

She recalls with much disdain how her friends who have moved to the UK would call her up and tell her to join them. They would tell her about all the facilities and opportunities awaiting her there, only if she would move. Multiple times in the book, Paudel shares the sentiment that there is no lack of nurses in the UK; if she does not go, someone else definitely will. Where there is a lack is in Jumla, and there, no one is willing to go. This is her reason for going. Jumla needs her; the United Kingdom does not.

At times, it feels to Paudel that not going to Jumla would almost be immoral. It would be a betrayal of the people there, for whom her services could be and are the difference between life and death. Her retelling of the death of a pregnant woman in her arms, just days after she arrives in Jumla, is a particularly jarring one.

The question then asked of the reader is what their duty is and to whom their duty is. As someone with the ability to help, to not help is simply wrong action—the way Paudel sees it.

In the middle of a civil war, with increasing Maoist activity around Jumla, Paudel’s friends, her siblings, her mother and even her father, who had sown the seed of Jumla in her mind, all plead with her not to go. When the Maoist attack on Khalanga does come, and Paudel’s employers come to airlift her out of the district. She leaves, but as she does, she laments for the Jumlis who have no safe place to which to flee.

Paudel comes back to Khalanga four weeks after the attack. When writing her book in 2013, she was still actively working for the betterment of the people of Jumla. She wins awards and recognition for her work; she manages to raise tens of lakhs and help thousands of families.

It is difficult not to feel hypocritical or greedy when reading ‘Jumla: A Nurse’s Story’. Here is a woman of such drive and education and courage, someone who could create a comfortable life for herself no matter where she went and what she did.

But she chooses to live with the poor and the downtrodden, to eat and sleep and live like them and with them, even when she could very well end up dead. Throughout my read of the book, I was in awe of Paudel’s sheer selflessness and sense of duty. It very rarely felt like she did anything for herself.

She has unshakeable resolve and an ability to work through the darkness of doubt and uncertainty. And in the wake of life’s rat race, in the race to secure your passport and then your acceptance to a foreign university, then your visa and finally your ticket away from Nepal, Paudel’s book is a discomforting yet necessary read that asks the reader to think about what they should do with their lives and why.______________________

Jumla: A Nurse's Story

Author: Radha Paudel

Year: 2013 (in Nepali); English translation in 2017

Publisher: Nepalaya
